explanations.explanation: Verse 2 says it plainly: "do not abandon my directive." The father calls his teaching sound, and then he asks his sons to stick with it. Walking away from good teaching is like leaving a perfect dough out on the counter all night. Stay with it, friend.

I get why this one looks right, but the verse never says that. What the father says is, "do not abandon my directive." Asking about something and walking away from it are two different things. I think a son who stays in the room is still listening.

Rushing sounds close, but the verse is about something else. The father says, "do not abandon my directive." It's about leaving his teaching behind, not about how fast you go through it. I've rushed plenty of batches myself, and speed was never the real problem. The problem was walking off and forgetting the timer.

Verse 3 says the father was once a son to his own father. Then verse 4 says, "he taught me and said…" and the words that follow are what the father is now passing along. So the teaching is coming down from his own dad. That's three generations in one little passage, friend.

Not quite, because the father isn't making this up fresh. Verse 3 says he was once a son to his own father, and verse 4 says, "he taught me and said…" What follows is his father's teaching. So he's handing down what he received.

explanations.answer: Forget them or turn from them
explanations.explanation: Verse 5 says, "do not forget my words or turn from them." Grandpa wants his son to remember the words and to keep facing them. Forgetting and turning away are the two ways to lose them. Keep them close, friend.

explanations.answer: Hide them or keep them secret
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse says to hide anything. Grandpa says, "Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn from them." He wants the words remembered and followed. Words stuffed in a secret spot are no help to anybody, same as a recipe nobody can find.

explanations.answer: Change them or add to them
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention changing or adding to anything. Grandpa says, "do not forget my words or turn from them." His worry is that his son might lose the words, not that he'd rewrite them. Think of a family recipe you love. You'd rather remember it than tinker with it.

Verse 6 says, "love her, and she will guard you." Grandpa talks about wisdom like a person who looks out for whoever loves her. That's a pretty good bodyguard to have, friend. And she doesn't charge by the hour.
The word in verse 6 isn't "humble." Grandpa says, "love her, and she will guard you." Loving wisdom brings protection. Nothing in the verse says she cuts anybody down to size.
Close, but the verse says something different. Grandpa says, "love her, and she will guard you." Wisdom isn't trailing behind like a shadow here. She's watching over the one who loves her.

Verse 7 says, "And whatever you may acquire, gain understanding." Grandpa says to get wisdom, and then he adds understanding on top. No matter what else you pick up in life, that comes first. A full cookie jar is nice, but this is the part worth getting.

Grandpa really does say this. Verse 7 reads, "And whatever you may acquire, gain understanding." He never tells his son to skip understanding for something else. It's right there next to wisdom, so both get the spotlight.

Verse 9 says, "She will set a garland of grace on your head." A garland is a wreath for the head, and this one is made of grace. Then comes a crown of beauty too. I think I'd wear that over my chef's hat, friend, and I'd make it work.
No turban shows up in this passage. Verse 9 says, "She will set a garland of grace on your head." It's a wreath, and it's made of grace. A crown of beauty follows right after.

A diadem sounds fancy, but that's not the wording here. Verse 9 says, "She will set a garland of grace on your head." The crown comes next, and the verse calls it "a crown of beauty." Grace first, then the crown.

Verse 10 says, "Listen, my son, and receive my words, and the years of your life will be many." The father ties his words to a long life. Listening counts for a lot here. It's just ears and a willing heart, friend.
No inheritance comes up in this verse. The father says, "Listen, my son, and receive my words, and the years of your life will be many." What he promises is a long life. Money is never mentioned.

Sons are mentioned in this passage, but not as the reward. Verse 10 says, "Listen, my son, and receive my words, and the years of your life will be many." The promise is about the years of his own life. Somebody else's family tree isn't part of it.

The father says the opposite. Verse 12 reads, "When you walk, your steps will not be impeded; when you run, you will not stumble." So on the way of wisdom, running doesn't end in a stumble. Walking is covered too, friend.

Right, because the father says the opposite. Verse 12 reads, "When you walk, your steps will not be impeded; when you run, you will not stumble." So the paths of wisdom are clear for walking and for running. No stumbling is mentioned at all.
Verse 13 says, "Guard it, for it is your life." The father isn't calling instruction a nice extra. He's calling it your life. That's worth guarding, friend.
The father never mentions comfort. Verse 13 says, "Hold on to instruction; do not let go. Guard it, for it is your life." Instruction isn't about being cozy. It's about your life.
That word never shows up here. Verse 13 says, "Guard it, for it is your life." He isn't handing his son a chore. He's telling him what instruction is to him.

The father says no such thing. Verse 14 says, "Do not set foot on the path of the wicked," and verse 15 adds, "Avoid it; do not travel on it. Turn from it and pass on by." He doesn't say a little time on it is fine. He says don't even set foot on it.

He doesn't allow it at all. Verse 14 says, "Do not set foot on the path of the wicked," and verse 15 adds, "Avoid it; do not travel on it. Turn from it and pass on by." Not a toe on that road, friend. Just keep walking past it.

Verse 16 says, "they are deprived of slumber until they make someone fall." That one is heavy, because it's about people being hurt. The father is showing his son what the wicked path is really like. I think that's why he says to stay far away from it.

Silver isn't in this verse. It says, "they are deprived of slumber until they make someone fall." The wicked here lose sleep over making others fall, not over money. It's a heavy picture, so the father says to steer clear.

Arguments don't come up in this verse. It says, "they are deprived of slumber until they make someone fall." That's a much heavier thing than losing a debate. I think the father wants his son to see what's at stake on that road.

Verse 18 says the path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, "shining brighter and brighter until midday." So the light keeps growing. It starts small and ends up full strength. That's a path getting clearer the longer you walk it, friend.
It goes the other direction. Verse 18 says the path of the righteous shines "brighter and brighter until midday." The father's picture is of light growing, not dimming. Evening doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: It flickers and then goes out
explanations.explanation: This light doesn't go out. Verse 18 says it keeps "shining brighter and brighter until midday." Dawn is the start, and the light only grows from there. I like that this road gets brighter the farther you go.

It's the other way around. Verse 19 says, "But the way of the wicked is like the darkest gloom; they do not know what makes them stumble." They're in the dark and can't even tell what trips them. That's the opposite of knowing exactly.

Right, they don't know. Verse 19 says, "But the way of the wicked is like the darkest gloom; they do not know what makes them stumble." They keep stumbling in the dark and can't see what's tripping them. That's a hard road, friend.
Verse 21 says, "keep them within your heart." The father wants his words down deep, not just in your ears. Then they go where you go. A heart makes a good pocket, friend.

The verse doesn't say tent. It says, "Do not lose sight of them; keep them within your heart." The words are meant to live inside the person. A tent can be packed up and left behind, and the heart goes with you.

A storehouse isn't in this verse. It says, "keep them within your heart." The father wants his words inside you, where you can't lose track of them. Stuff left in a storehouse tends to get forgotten, like a cookie box in the back of the pantry.

Verse 22 says, "For they are life to those who find them, and health to the whole body." So the father's words are life to the ones who find them, and health to the whole body as well. That's both at once, friend.
The father does say this. Verse 22 reads, "For they are life to those who find them, and health to the whole body." So the words bring life, and they also bring health to the whole body.

explanations.answer: Springs of life flow from it
explanations.explanation: Verse 23 says, "Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life." The reason is right there in the verse. Springs of life come out of the heart. So it's worth watching over, friend.
The verse gives a different reason. It says, "Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life." Nothing here says the heart breaks easily. The point is what flows out of it.

explanations.answer: Others will try to steal it
explanations.explanation: Thieves aren't mentioned in this verse. It says, "Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life." The reason is what comes out of the heart. Life flows from there.
Verse 25 says, "Let your eyes look forward; fix your gaze straight ahead." The father wants eyes pointed where the feet are going. Keep your eyes on the road and you stay on the road.

Looking around isn't what the father says. Verse 25 says, "Let your eyes look forward; fix your gaze straight ahead." He wants the gaze fixed, not wandering. A wandering eye is how you end up walking into a doorframe.
Nothing about looking behind here. Verse 25 says, "Let your eyes look forward; fix your gaze straight ahead." The eyes go the same way as the road. That's forward, friend.
Verse 27 says, "Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your feet away from evil." Stay on the level path and keep going straight. No drifting to either side, friend.

explanations.answer: Don't stop to rest along it
explanations.explanation: Resting isn't mentioned at all. Verse 27 says, "Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your feet away from evil." The warning is about drifting off the path. It says nothing against a breather.

Walking alone doesn't come up in this verse. It says, "Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your feet away from evil." The warning is about leaving the path to either side. Keep your feet on it.
